meta.disclaimer: Curated scientific reconstructions and projections. Entirely separate from the live ephemeris clock: planetary positions are only computable ~±3,000 years from now, so these eras morph the APPEARANCE and swap in sourced facts — they do not compute positions.
meta.morphs: Procedural only (shader tints, whitening, luminance-keyed ocean overlay, ring-opacity fade, scale changes, cloud/atmosphere parameter blends of existing vendored textures). No new image assets. Visuals are artist's impressions guided by the cited science.
meta.sources_verified: 2026-07-11: Saturn ring-rain figures verified against the linked NASA article; remaining values are standard published figures cited per epoch. 2026-07-14 (H17): Venus early-water debate and Moon chronology figures are standard published values cited per epoch; lunar recession rate 3.82 cm/yr per NASA lunar laser ranging.

Mars.name: Noachian Mars
Mars.source: NASA Mars Exploration Program; Carr & Head (2010), 'Geologic history of Mars', EPSL
Mars.desc: Mars at its most Earth-like: a thicker atmosphere, rain-carved valley networks, crater lakes, and possibly a sea covering much of the northern lowlands. The clay minerals rovers find today formed in this water-rich era. Ocean extent shown is an artist's impression — its existence is still debated.

Mars.name: Hesperian Mars
Mars.source: NASA Mars Exploration Program; Carr & Head (2010)
Mars.desc: The great drying. Volcanoes resurfaced whole regions, catastrophic floods carved the giant outflow channels, and the remaining water turned acidic and sulfate-rich as the atmosphere thinned.

Mars.name: Amazonian Mars (Now)
Mars.desc: Today's Mars: cold, hyper-arid, a thin CO₂ atmosphere under 1% of Earth's pressure, global dust, and water surviving as polar ice and subsurface deposits.

Saturn.name: Rings today (Now)
Saturn.source: NASA/Cassini; O'Donoghue et al. (2019), Icarus — rings likely young (≲100 Myr, debated)
Saturn.desc: The full bright ring system — mostly water ice, thinner than a sheet of paper relative to its size. Cassini-era evidence suggests the rings are geologically YOUNG, likely less than ~100 million years old, though their age is still debated.

Saturn.name: Rings fading
Saturn.source: NASA (2018): 'Saturn is Losing Its Rings at Worst-Case-Scenario Rate'; O'Donoghue et al. (2019), Icarus
Saturn.desc: 'Ring rain': the magnetic field pulls charged ice grains down into Saturn's atmosphere — enough water to fill an Olympic pool every half hour. The inner rings drain first. The mechanism is measured; the exact timing is a broad range.

Saturn.name: Ringless Saturn
Saturn.source: NASA (2018) / O'Donoghue et al. (2019): <100 Myr worst case, ~300 Myr from ring rain alone; some studies argue longer — timing debated
Saturn.desc: Saturn without its rings — a plain gas giant, as it likely was for most of its 4.5-billion-year history if the rings really are young. Future observers may know the rings only from our era's photographs.

Venus.name: Early Venus — a water world?
Venus.time: ~4–3 billion years ago (some models: until ~700 million years ago)
Venus.source: Way et al. (2016), GRL — climate models allow shallow oceans and temperate conditions for ~2–3 Gyr; BUT Turbet et al. (2021), Nature, argues day-side clouds kept early Venus too hot for water to ever condense — genuinely unresolved
Venus.desc: Did Venus once have oceans? Climate models by Way and colleagues suggest a slowly rotating young Venus could have stayed temperate, with shallow seas, for billions of years. More recent modeling (Turbet 2021) counters that water may NEVER have rained out onto the surface at all. Both views are current science — the blue ocean world shown here is one debated possibility, not a consensus. Artist's impression.

Venus.name: Runaway greenhouse
Venus.time: onset uncertain — sometime between ~3.5 billion and ~700 million years ago
Venus.source: Ingersoll (1969), JAS — runaway-greenhouse mechanism; Donahue et al. (1982), Science — Venus's deuterium/hydrogen ratio ~150× Earth's, the fingerprint of an ocean's worth of water lost to space; NASA Venus overview
Venus.desc: However it began, the outcome is written in Venus's air: as the brightening Sun evaporated any surface water, water vapor's own greenhouse effect fed the warming, sunlight split the vapor and the hydrogen escaped to space. With no water left to weather rock, CO₂ piled up in the atmosphere unchecked. The mechanism is established physics; the timing is not.

Venus.name: Venus today (Now)
Venus.desc: The hottest planet: ~465 °C at the surface — hot enough to melt lead — under ~92 bars of CO₂, wrapped in globe-spanning clouds of sulfuric acid. A cautionary twin of Earth, and the reason 'runaway greenhouse' is a term at all.

Moon.name: Birth: the magma ocean
Moon.source: NASA — Theia giant-impact hypothesis; Apollo samples: the anorthosite highland crust crystallized from a global magma ocean (LPI)
Moon.desc: A Mars-sized body, Theia, struck the young Earth; the Moon coalesced from the incandescent debris. For its first tens of millions of years it was covered by a global ocean of molten rock — the pale highland crust we see today is the 'scum' that floated and froze on top. It hung enormous in Earth's sky, orbiting many times closer than now. Artist's impression.

Moon.name: Heavy bombardment
Moon.source: Apollo impact-melt ages define the era; whether it was a distinct 'Late Heavy Bombardment' spike or the tail of a smooth decline is actively debated (Boehnke & Harrison 2016, PNAS)
Moon.desc: Giant impacts excavated the vast basins — Imbrium, Serenitatis, Crisium — that still shape the Moon's face, while smaller strikes saturated the surface with craters. Note the honest caveat: the cratering happened, but whether it came as a late SPIKE (the classic 'Late Heavy Bombardment') or a long steady decline is still argued. Shown pre-maria: pale, uniformly battered highlands. Artist's impression.

Moon.name: Mare volcanism
Moon.source: NASA/LPI — Apollo mare basalt sample ages; peak mare emplacement ~3.5–3.0 Gya
Moon.desc: Radioactive heating melted the Moon's interior and basaltic lava flooded the great impact basins, freezing into the dark plains — the maria, or 'seas' — that draw the face of the Man in the Moon. The warm tint shown suggests the era's active flows. Artist's impression.

Moon.name: The Moon today (Now)
Moon.desc: Geologically quiet for billions of years: the same maria, highlands, and rays of the young crater Tycho that every human who ever lived has looked up at.

Moon.name: Drifting away
Moon.source: NASA — lunar laser ranging against the Apollo retroreflectors measures the Moon receding 3.8 cm per year; tidal transfer of Earth's spin angular momentum
Moon.desc: Laser pulses bounced off Apollo-era mirrors show the Moon spiraling outward ~3.8 cm every year, fed by Earth's tides — and Earth's day slowly lengthening in exchange. In the distant future the Moon will appear too small to fully cover the Sun, and total solar eclipses will end. Shown smaller in the sky, as a far-future observer would see it.

Sun.name: Young Sun
Sun.source: NASA Sun overview; standard solar-system formation chronology (CAI ages ~4.567 Gyr)
Sun.desc: The newborn Sun, freshly ignited inside its collapsing gas cloud: about 30% dimmer than today but far more magnetically violent, flaring constantly while the planets assembled from the surrounding disk.

Sun.name: Middle age (Now)
Sun.desc: A stable G2 main-sequence star, roughly halfway through its hydrogen-burning life. It has already brightened ~30% since its youth and continues to brighten slowly.

Sun.name: Brighter Sun
Sun.source: Standard stellar evolution; Kasting (1988) moist-greenhouse threshold; Schröder & Connon Smith (2008), MNRAS
Sun.desc: About 10% more luminous than today — enough, models project, to push Earth into a moist greenhouse where the oceans slowly evaporate. The Sun itself looks only subtly different: slightly larger, slightly whiter.

Sun.name: Red giant
Sun.source: Schröder & Connon Smith (2008), MNRAS; NASA/ESA stellar evolution
Sun.desc: Hydrogen exhausted, the Sun swells hundreds of times wider, engulfing Mercury and Venus — Earth's survival is genuinely uncertain. Shown here far smaller than true scale: a real red giant Sun would reach roughly toward Earth's orbit.

Sun.name: White dwarf
Sun.source: Standard stellar evolution (NASA/ESA); Schröder & Connon Smith (2008)
Sun.desc: After shedding its outer layers as a planetary nebula, the Sun's exposed core remains: an Earth-sized ember of crystallizing carbon and oxygen, initially white-hot, cooling for eternity. Shown larger than true scale (a real white dwarf is ~100× smaller than the Sun).

Earth.name: Hadean Earth
Earth.source: USGS (age of Earth, 4.54 ± 0.05 Gyr); NASA — Moon-forming giant impact (Theia)
Earth.desc: A world of magma. Shortly after Earth assembled, a Mars-sized body (Theia) struck it — the debris became the Moon, which loomed enormous in the sky over a glowing magma ocean. No continents, no oceans, no life.

Earth.name: Early oceans & first life
Earth.source: NASA Astrobiology; zircon evidence of early oceans (~4.0+ Gya); stromatolite fossils (~3.5 Gya)
Earth.desc: A water world under an orange, oxygen-free sky: global oceans dotted with volcanic islands, tides far stronger under a much closer Moon, and — in those waters — the first microbial life.

Earth.name: Snowball Earth
Earth.source: Huronian glaciation (~2.4 Gya) and Cryogenian Sturtian/Marinoan glaciations (~717–635 Mya) — established geology; fully global 'hard snowball' extent still debated
Earth.desc: Ice from pole to pole — or nearly so. At least twice, runaway glaciation wrapped the planet in ice for millions of years; volcanic CO₂ eventually thawed it. The debate is whether a belt of open equatorial water ('slushball') survived.

Earth.name: Earth today (Now)
Earth.desc: The only world known to host life — oceans, continents, an oxygen atmosphere, and city lights on the night side.

Earth.name: Evaporating oceans
Earth.source: Kasting (1988) moist-greenhouse models; standard solar-brightening projections (Schröder & Connon Smith 2008)
Earth.desc: The slowly brightening Sun tips Earth into a moist greenhouse: oceans evaporate into a thick steam atmosphere, water is lost to space, and the surface trends toward a hot desert world. Complex life's era ends long before the red-giant Sun arrives.
